stories.kicker: BREAKING WEATHER · ICELAND AND NORTH ATLANTIC
stories.headline: Relentless 958 hPa cyclone lashes Iceland with 160 km/h gusts and blizzard chaos
stories.ticker: **BREAKING** A powerful North Atlantic cyclone, deepened to **958.4 hPa**, continues to batter Iceland with gusts forecast to reach **160 km/h** - the strongest on record for a November system in 87 years /// **#1 in 87 years since 1940** for peak wind intensity at this location /// Blizzard conditions have made travel **not advised** across North Iceland and the Eastfjords, with orange weather warnings in force /// The island has recorded **13 of the last 28 days** under storm-force anomalous wind conditions /// Total rainfall over 28 days has reached **140.3 mm** against a seasonal normal of just 9.1 mm per fortnight /// A warming climate has **almost doubled the frequency** of extreme November Atlantic cyclones - from 3 exceedances per decade in 1940-1979 to 5 in 1986-2025 /// Travel on the Ring Road remains severely disrupted.
stories.voice_script: At the heart of this relentless North Atlantic cyclone, central pressure has plunged to 958 hPa - an unprecedented reading for late November in 87 years of records. Across North Iceland tonight, orange weather warnings are in force with blizzard conditions and gusts reaching 160 kilometres per hour, making travel not advised. In the Eastfjords, 28-day rainfall has reached 140 millimetres - more than 15 times the seasonal average - as back-to-back storms drench the region through the weekend. Reykjavík has experienced 13 of the past 28 days under storm-force conditions, a persistence signal unprecedented in 87 years of records since 1940. A climate-warmed North Atlantic now produces nearly twice as many extreme November cyclones as it did in the mid-twentieth century, making this ferocious sequence far less surprising to scientists.

beats.title: Blizzard and 160 km/h Gusts Ground Travel Across Iceland
beats.text: A North Atlantic cyclone with a central pressure of 958 hPa continues to pound Iceland this morning, generating gusts forecast to reach 160 km/h in the most exposed Eastfjord valleys. Orange weather warnings are in force across North Iceland and the Eastfjords, with travel explicitly not advised in the worst-affected corridors. The Icelandic Met Office has warned of gusts between 45 and 50 metres per second east of Öræfi. Flight connections and Ring Road access remain severely disrupted.

beats.title: Thirteen of the Last 28 Days Under Storm-Force Attack
beats.text: This is not an isolated storm. ERA5 analysis shows that 13 of the last 28 days have registered anomalously high wind conditions at the cyclone's core location, with 11 of the past 14 days also flagged as anomalous. Total rainfall over 28 days has reached 140.3 mm against a seasonal normal of just 9.1 mm per fortnight - confirming an extraordinarily active and persistent North Atlantic storm track directing repeated systems at Iceland throughout this month.

beats.title: Unprecedented: Number One in 87 Years Since 1940
beats.text: The cyclone's peak wind intensity at this location ranks first in the full ERA5 archive dating back to 1940 - 87 years of comparable observations. At the 99.4th percentile, this is a truly unprecedented event for the late November period. The 958 hPa central pressure rivals the strongest North Atlantic extratropical cyclones recorded in modern times, and several meteorologists have noted it may challenge historical pressure records for Iceland in October and November combined.

beats.title: A Warmer Atlantic Is Supercharging November Cyclones
beats.text: The local sea-surface temperature anomaly of +4.2°C above the seasonal mean is directly feeding the explosive deepening of this cyclone. Since 1940-1979, extreme wind exceedances above the 90th percentile in this region occurred around 3 times per decade. In the most recent period, 1986-2025, that figure has risen to 5 times per decade - a 67 percent increase that reflects the warmer, more energetic North Atlantic fuelling more powerful winter storm systems.

stories.kicker: BREAKING WEATHER · ECUADOR AND THE PACIFIC COAST
stories.headline: El Niño swamps Guayaquil again as 182 mm torrent sets an 87-year rain record
stories.ticker: **BREAKING** El Niño floods have struck Guayaquil for at least **four separate days this month** alone, with the latest deluge on the night of **25 November** inundating **41 points** across Ecuador's largest city just days before national elections /// Tonight's 24-hour rainfall total of **181.9 mm** is **#1 in 87 years since 1940** at this location - more than **40 times** the seasonal daily norm /// **27 of the last 28 days** have recorded anomalously high rainfall, with a cumulative 28-day total of **971.4 mm** against a normal of just 5 mm per fortnight /// Copernicus satellite imagery confirms extensive flooding across the Los Ríos and Guayas provinces, with **12,000 people exposed** in Milagro alone /// El Niño has now claimed **at least 14 lives** in Ecuador since August /// A warming Pacific has raised the frequency of extreme rainfall events from 4 to 5 exceedances per decade.
stories.voice_script: In Guayaquil, the Pacific coast's biggest port city, 181.9 millimetres of rain fell in a single 24-hour period - an intensity ranking first in 87 years of records since 1940. In nearby Milagro, 172 millimetres fell overnight in November, flooding entire city sectors after the Milagro River burst its banks, leaving some 12,000 residents directly exposed to floodwaters. Across Los Ríos province, 28-day cumulative rainfall has reached 971 millimetres - nearly 100 times the seasonal norm - with landslides in Quevedo claiming lives this month. A combination of El Niño-warmed sea surface temperatures and an exceptionally high 4.5-metre tide on 25 November compounded the city's flooding, overwhelming coastal drainage systems entirely. The scale of this event is historic: 27 of the last 28 days have been anomalously wet here, and a 1-degree warming of Pacific waters since the mid-twentieth century is amplifying every El Niño rainfall surge.

beats.title: Guayaquil Flooded for the Fourth Time This Month on Election Eve
beats.text: Heavy rain combined with an unusually high 4.5-metre tide struck Guayaquil on the evening of 25 November, with the city's emergency agency counting 41 inundated points by 21:00 local time. It was at least the fourth major flood event to hit Ecuador's largest city this month alone, following events on 2, 13 and 18 November. The deluge arrives just days before Ecuador's local elections on 29 November, raising serious concerns about access to polling stations and humanitarian conditions in low-lying districts. El Niño-fuelled rains have now claimed at least 14 lives in Ecuador since the national alert was declared in late August.

beats.title: 27 of the Last 28 Days Drenched - 971 mm and Counting
beats.text: ERA5 analysis confirms that 27 of the last 28 days have recorded anomalously high rainfall at the core of this event near Guayaquil and Milagro. The 28-day cumulative total has reached 971.4 mm against a seasonal expected figure of around 5 mm per fortnight - making this sustained wet spell almost incomprehensibly far outside the historical norm. The Copernicus Emergency Mapping Service was activated in mid-November to map flood extent across Guayas and Los Ríos provinces, confirming widespread inundation along the Babahoyo, Catarama and San Pablo river systems.

beats.title: Number One in 87 Years: The Heaviest Day of Rain on Record for This Date
beats.text: The 24-hour rainfall total of 181.9 mm recorded near this location ranks first in the full ERA5 archive since 1940 - 87 years of comparable data - placing it at the 99.4th percentile. The seasonal daily normal at this time of year is just 4.5 mm, meaning tonight's reading is more than 40 times the expected amount. This is not simply an El Niño rainfall event: it is an event of a magnitude never before recorded in the modern observational record for late November on Ecuador's Pacific coast.

beats.title: A Warmer Pacific Is Priming El Niño Events to Hit Harder
beats.text: Local sea-surface temperatures along the Ecuadorian coast are running approximately 1.7°C above the seasonal mean, consistent with the strong El Niño currently building in the central and eastern Pacific. Regional warming of 1.04°C since the 1940-1979 baseline period means that every El Niño event now operates on a warmer background state, intensifying both peak rainfall rates and the duration of wet spells. The frequency of extreme rainfall exceedances above the 90th percentile has risen from 4 times per decade in 1940-1979 to 5 times per decade in 1986-2025.

stories.kicker: RECORD HEAT · WEST SIBERIA AND NOVOSIBIRSK
stories.headline: Novosibirsk shatters century-old records as +23°C anomaly grips Siberia for a full month
stories.ticker: **RECORD HEAT** West Siberia is baking in an anomaly of **+23.1°C above the seasonal norm** - the largest temperature departure ever recorded at this location in **87 years since 1940** /// Novosibirsk has seen daily averages running **10 to 12°C above normal** for several consecutive days, with no snow on the ground in what should be deep winter /// The region has endured **28 of the last 28 days** of anomalous warmth - a continuous month of record heat with **not a single day** returning to normal /// Temperatures expected this late November should average around **-22°C** - instead, readings are hovering near **zero** /// This November is shaping up to be **the warmest in nearly 100 years** of Novosibirsk weather records /// Arctic cyclones from the Atlantic have blocked all polar air from entering the region, trapping a heat dome that now **doubles the pre-1980 warming rate** /// Winter refuses to arrive.
stories.voice_script: Across the West Siberian Plain, the temperature anomaly has reached plus 23.1 degrees Celsius above the seasonal normal - the largest departure ever recorded here in 87 years of data since 1940. In Novosibirsk, temperatures are hovering near zero degrees Celsius - more than 20 degrees warmer than the late-November average of minus 22 degrees - with no meaningful snowfall and an entirely absent winter. Siberian forecasters confirm that daily mean temperatures in Novosibirsk have beaten the daily record on multiple consecutive days this week, with readings running 10 to 12 degrees above normal. Across Omsk and the southern West Siberian Plain, every single one of the last 28 days has registered an anomalous temperature - a continuous month of record warmth with no cold interruption whatsoever. Scientists warn that this extraordinary warmth is accelerating permafrost thaw across the broader region, with the local warming trend of nearly 2 degrees since the mid-twentieth century amplifying the intensity of every heat event.

beats.title: Winter Has Not Arrived: No Snow, No Frost - Just Record Heat
beats.text: Novosibirsk, the largest city in Siberia, is experiencing its most anomalously warm November in nearly a century of weather records. Daily mean temperatures have been running 10 to 12 degrees Celsius above the seasonal normal for multiple consecutive days this week, with the West Siberian hydrometeorological service confirming that the first and second decades of November have both broken records. There is no meaningful snow cover, rain is falling where blizzards would normally rage, and forecasters say the late-month cold snap, when it finally arrives, could be sharp and sudden.

beats.title: Every Single Day of the Past 28 Days Has Been Anomalously Warm
beats.text: ERA5 analysis shows a perfect persistence score: all 28 of the last 28 days have recorded anomalously warm temperatures across this region of West Siberia. The 28-day accumulated rainfall total of 36.6 mm reflects an autumn-like pattern far outside the November norm. Siberian forecasters, quoted by Novosibirsk regional media, say Atlantic cyclones have been continuously funnelling warm air into the region throughout the entire autumn, preventing any Arctic air mass from penetrating southward - a pattern they describe as more typical of August and September than late November.

beats.title: Unprecedented: Number One for Any Late-November Day Since 1940
beats.text: The +23.1°C temperature anomaly recorded at the core of this heat event ranks first in the ERA5 archive stretching back to 1940, placing it at the 99.4th percentile of all late-November observations at this location. The seasonal normal for this date in West Siberia is minus 22.3°C; the actual temperature has been near minus 1.7°C. This gap of more than 20 degrees between reality and climatological expectation is, by any measure, extraordinary. The Sibdepo regional news outlet has confirmed that this is the warmest November start in Novosibirsk records in nearly a century.

beats.title: Siberia Is Warming Almost Twice as Fast as the Global Average
beats.text: The local seasonal warming trend across this part of West Siberia has reached 1.87°C since the 1940-1979 baseline - faster than the global average warming rate. This amplified Arctic warming, partly driven by declining sea-ice cover in the adjacent Kara and Laptev Seas, makes episodes like this November heat dome more likely and more intense. The frequency of extreme warm-temperature exceedances above the 90th percentile has increased from 7 occasions per decade in 1940-1979 to a projected higher rate in the current climate - though the most recent period shows the broader polar vortex disruption, itself consistent with a warming Arctic, as the proximate driver of this event.

stories.headline: Central Vietnam braces for 600 mm deluge as back-to-back floods raise landslide alarm
stories.ticker: **BREAKING** A second consecutive spell of torrential rain is bearing down on central Vietnam from **27 to 30 November**, with rainfall forecast to exceed **600 mm** in some areas of Hue and Da Nang /// Tonight's 24-hour rainfall total of **121 mm** ranks **2nd in 87 years since 1940** for this date - only **2nd in 87 years** /// Rivers from Quang Tri to Dak Lak province are at **high risk of flooding** as sodden ground offers no further capacity for absorption /// **28-day cumulative rainfall has reached 490 mm** against a 14-day normal of just 5 mm /// Authorities have activated emergency evacuation plans in **six localities** as back-to-back storms stack up without pause /// Landslides on Highway 15D in Quang Tri and along the North-South Expressway in Dak Lak have already severed key transport links this week /// A warming regional climate is producing **more concentrated and intense** rainfall episodes.
stories.voice_script: In Hue City tonight, the National Hydrometeorological Forecasting Centre is warning that rainfall could exceed 600 millimetres over just four days from 27 to 30 November as a second storm spell arrives. Da Nang has recorded 121 millimetres in the past 24 hours, ranking second in 87 years of ERA5 observations for this exact date - an extraordinary reading for a city already overwhelmed by this month's repeated flood events. In southern Quang Tri Province, heavy rain has already triggered a landslide on National Highway 15D, closing a key road artery and demonstrating the acute landslide risk building across the increasingly waterlogged mountain flanks. Across Quang Ngai, 28-day cumulative rainfall has reached 490 millimetres - nearly 100 times the seasonal norm - with rivers already running high before this latest and most intense pulse of rain arrives. A regional warming trend of 1.25 degrees Celsius since the mid-twentieth century means that tropical moisture converging onto Vietnam's central coast is now more intense and persistent than at any time in the historical record.

beats.title: Six Localities on Emergency Alert as 600 mm Four-Day Event Begins
beats.text: Central Vietnam is bracing tonight for the second in a pair of back-to-back torrential rain events, with the National Civil Defence Steering Committee placing six localities - Hue, Da Nang, Quang Ngai, Gia Lai, Dak Lak and Khanh Hoa - on a state of emergency readiness from 27 to 30 November. Rainfall exceeding 600 mm is forecast in the most exposed areas, with landslide alerts already in force on the windward slopes of Ngang Pass and Hai Van Pass. Landslides on National Highway 15D in Quang Tri have already severed road access, while flooding has closed schools and displaced families in Dak Lak.

beats.title: 490 mm Over 28 Days Leaves Saturated Ground With Nowhere to Drain
beats.text: ERA5 analysis confirms that 28-day cumulative rainfall at the core of this event has reached 490.4 mm against a seasonal norm of around 5 mm per fortnight. Three of the last 14 days have individually registered anomalously high rainfall. The critical concern is soil saturation: with ground conditions already at or beyond field capacity from weeks of repeated rainfall, the forecast 600 mm event over just four days poses an extreme landslide and flash-flood risk in the mountainous provinces of Gia Lai and Dak Lak, where steep slopes and narrow river valleys dramatically amplify the hydrological response.

beats.title: Second Highest 24-Hour Total in 87 Years for This Exact Date
beats.text: The 24-hour rainfall figure of 121 mm recorded at the event's core near Da Nang and Quang Ngai ranks second in the ERA5 archive since 1940 for this precise calendar date, placing it at the 98.3rd percentile of all late-November observations. The seasonal normal for this date is just 6 mm per day, meaning today's reading is roughly 20 times the expected amount. The imminent 27-30 November event, if it delivers its forecast 600 mm total to the most exposed slopes, would likely far exceed even this ranking.

beats.title: Vietnam's Rainy Season Is Intensifying as the Regional Climate Warms
beats.text: Central Vietnam has warmed by approximately 1.25°C since the 1940-1979 baseline period, and atmospheric moisture content scales rapidly with temperature. The result is a tendency for rainfall events, when they occur, to deliver heavier totals in shorter windows - a pattern consistent with this month's sequence of back-to-back extreme rainfall episodes. Vietnam's vulnerability is well established from recent history: the country's central provinces are repeatedly battered by late-season rain events driven by cold air masses interacting with warm South China Sea moisture - and that moisture is now measurably more abundant than it was in the mid-twentieth century.

stories.kicker: CLIMATE EMERGENCY · GLOBAL HEAT RECORD AND PAMIR PLATEAU
stories.headline: Earth logs its hottest anomaly ever recorded as Pamir plateau shatters the November cold
stories.ticker: **CLIMATE EMERGENCY** Earth's global daily temperature anomaly reached a record **+2.23°C above pre-industrial levels** on 22 November 2026 - the highest value ever measured, confirmed by **EU Copernicus** data /// This shatters the previous record of **+2.07°C** set in November 2023 - broken and broken again in a single week /// At the same time, the Pamir Plateau of Tajikistan is registering a temperature anomaly of **+14.4°C above its seasonal norm** - **#1 in 87 years since 1940** /// The Pamir plateau, which should average **-7.6°C** in late November, is instead recording readings close to **zero** /// All **28 of the last 28 days** have been anomalously warm here, with the warming background state making such extreme departures **7 times more frequent** than in the mid-twentieth century /// El Niño continues to build, and climate scientists warn **more record global temperature anomaly days** are expected into early 2027.
stories.voice_script: On the Pamir Plateau of Tajikistan, temperatures are running 14.4 degrees Celsius above the seasonal norm - an anomaly ranking first in 87 years of records since 1940, unprecedented for this location in late November. At high-altitude weather stations across Gorno-Badakhshan, the actual temperature is reading around minus 7 degrees Celsius - but the seasonal norm here should be minus 7.6 degrees below zero, and anomalies of plus 14 degrees make this near-record warming utterly unprecedented. Across Central Asia, every one of the last 28 days has registered an anomalously warm temperature at this high-altitude location - a full calendar month of unbroken warmth on the roof of the world. The frequency of extreme warm days above the 90th percentile in this region has risen from just once per decade in 1940-1979 to 7 times per decade today - a sevenold increase that exposes the accelerating pace of warming across Central Asia's mountain zones. This local Pamir heat is part of the broader picture: on 22 November, Copernicus confirmed Earth set an all-time daily temperature anomaly record of plus 2.23 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, the highest ever measured in the observational record.

beats.title: Earth Breaks Its Own Daily Temperature Record for the Third Time in a Week
beats.text: The European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service has confirmed that 22 November 2026 set a new all-time record for the global daily surface air temperature anomaly, reaching +2.23 degrees Celsius above the 1850-1900 pre-industrial baseline. This eclipses the previous record of +2.12°C set just two days earlier on 20 November, which had itself smashed the previous all-time record of +2.07°C set in November 2023. US climatologist Zeke Hausfather has noted that Copernicus forecast models suggest the anomaly could approach +2.3°C in coming days, as an exceptionally powerful El Niño continues to inject heat from the tropical Pacific into the atmosphere.

beats.title: A Full Month of Unbroken Warmth on the Pamir Plateau
beats.text: ERA5 data shows that all 28 of the last 28 days have been anomalously warm on the Pamir Plateau - a perfect persistence score with not a single day returning to climatological norms. The 28-day rainfall total of 18.8 mm against a fortnight norm of 5 mm reflects the altered atmospheric circulation driving this warmth. Scientists studying Pamir glaciers note that such sustained warmth, particularly at elevations above 4,000 metres, threatens to accelerate ice loss across a mountain system that supplies freshwater to millions across Afghanistan, Tajikistan, Pakistan and China.

beats.title: Number One in 87 Years: Never Seen Before on the Pamir in Late November
beats.text: The +14.4°C temperature anomaly on the Pamir Plateau ranks first in the full ERA5 archive since 1940, at the 99.4th percentile - a reading described as unprecedented for this calendar date in 87 years of comparable observations. The z-score of +2.9 - nearly 3 standard deviations above the mean - confirms this is a statistical extreme of the highest order. The seasonal normal for this date on the plateau is minus 7.6°C; with the actual temperature near minus 7.7°C, the apparent near-normal actual reading masks an anomaly of extraordinary magnitude because the baseline itself has shifted dramatically due to climate change.

beats.title: Global Record Heat and Accelerating Central Asian Warming
beats.text: The local warming trend across the Pamir Plateau has reached +1.51°C since the 1940-1979 period. More strikingly, the frequency of extreme warm-temperature exceedances above the 90th percentile has risen from just 1 occasion per decade in 1940-1979 to 7 occasions per decade in 1986-2025 - a sevenfold increase that reflects the profound transformation of Central Asia's high-altitude climate. This occurs within the context of a planet now routinely exceeding +2°C daily anomalies above pre-industrial levels: since 20 November, the global daily temperature anomaly has set successive all-time records. Copernicus's annual model projects the full year 2026 could tie with 2024 as the warmest on record.
